title: Undoing safely
objectives: Choose between restore, revert and reset for each kind of mistake
Move a commit made on main by accident onto its own branch

screens.prose: Your last commit, c4, broke the signal code. You made it a minute ago, on your own, and nobody else has it. You want main to look as if c4 never happened.

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

screens.question: Tap the commit main should point to.

hints.text: A branch is a label. Where would it point if c4 had never been made?
c4 was built on this commit.
Before c4, main pointed at c3. Moving the label back there leaves c4 out.

feedback.correct: Point main back at c3, c4's parent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the commit main pointed at just before c4.

byKey.first: That would drop c2 and c3 as well. Only c4 is bad, so go back one step.
byKey.c4: That is the bad commit itself. main must point before it.
byKey.c2: That drops c3 too, which was fine. Go back one step only.
byKey.main: Tap a commit, not a label.
byKey.HEAD: Tap a commit, not a label.

explain.text: Moving main back to c3 is what `git reset --hard HEAD~1` does: HEAD~1 means one parent back. c4 still exists, but no branch reaches it any more. The folder is rewritten to match c3.

canvas.caption: After `git reset --hard HEAD~1`: no label reaches c4

screens.prose:
There is a second way to undo c4. This command makes a **new** commit, c5, whose changes are exactly the opposite of c4's:

```sh
$ git revert HEAD
```

Git opens your editor with a message starting Revert; save and close it.

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

enter.caption: After `git revert HEAD`: c5 undoes c4

screens.question: Tap every commit main contains now.

hints.text: Follow the arrows back from main. Is any commit skipped?
c5 is built on c4.
From c5 the arrows run through c4, c3, c2 and c1. Nothing was removed.

feedback.correct: All five: the bad commit and its undoing are both in the history.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow every arrow back from main.

byKey.dropped: c4 is still there. revert adds a commit that cancels c4; it removes nothing.
byKey.c4: c4 is still there. revert adds a commit that cancels c4; it removes nothing.
byKey.c1: Keep following arrows back, all the way to c1.
byKey.HEAD: Tap only commits.

explain.text: main now holds c4 and also c5, which cancels it. The files match c3 again, but the history only grew. Nothing anyone else has seen was changed.

screens.prose: So **reset** moves a branch back, dropping commits from it. **revert** adds a commit that cancels one. Now suppose a colleague has already built risk-model on top of the bad c4.

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

screens.question: Which undo is safe on main?

options.text: `git revert HEAD`: add a commit that cancels c4
`git reset --hard HEAD~1`: move main back to c3
options.why: risk-model still contains c4. When it is merged back, c4 returns, and main's history no longer matches your colleague's.
restore works on files in your folder. It does not touch commits.
Deleting a colleague's branch label does not delete their work, and it is theirs to keep.

hints.text: Which method leaves every existing commit in place?
This commit sits on c4. Removing c4 from main does not remove it from here.
Revert changes nothing that exists; it only adds. That keeps main and risk-model in agreement.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Prefer the undo that only adds a commit.

byKey.reset: risk-model still contains c4. When it is merged back, c4 returns, and main's history no longer matches your colleague's.

explain.text: Revert adds c5 and changes no existing commit, so risk-model and main still share the same past. When risk-model is merged, c5 keeps c4 cancelled. Reset is for commits only you have.

screens.prose: `HEAD~1` means one parent back from the commit HEAD is on. `HEAD~2` means two parents back, and so on.

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

state.caption: HEAD is on main, at c5

screens.question: Tap the commit `HEAD~2` names.

hints.text: Start at the commit HEAD is on. Step back along one arrow, then another.
HEAD is on this commit. Steps start here.
One step from c5 is c4 (HEAD~1). Two steps is c3.

feedback.correct: Two parents back from c5 is c3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at c5 and follow two arrows.

byKey.counted-start: That is HEAD~1, one step back. Take one more.
byKey.too-far: You took three steps. Count the arrows from c5: c4 is one, c3 is two.
byKey.c5: That is HEAD itself, HEAD~0. Step back twice.
byKey.main: Tap a commit, not a label.
byKey.HEAD: Tap a commit, not a label.

explain.text: From c5, one arrow leads to c4 and a second to c3. So `HEAD~2` is c3. `git reset --hard HEAD~2` would move main back two commits.

screens.prose: Three tools, three kinds of mistake. `git restore` works on files you have not committed. `git revert` and `git reset` work on commits.

rows: You edited signal.py an hour ago, never committed, and want the last committed version back
A bad commit on main that colleagues have already built on
A bad commit made a minute ago, on your own branch, never shared

screens.question: Drag each command to the situation it fits.

hints.text: Which situation involves no commit at all?
Situation A has nothing committed, so neither commit tool applies.
A: restore the file. B: revert, since others have the commit. C: reset, since only you have it.

feedback.correct: restore for files, revert for shared commits, reset for private ones.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. First ask: is there a commit? Then ask: has anyone else got it?

byKey.restore: restore throws away uncommitted edits to a file. Only situation A has no commit.
byKey.revert: revert is the safe undo for a commit others already have. That is situation B.
byKey.reset: reset moves a branch back, rewriting it. Use it only where nobody else has the commit: situation C.

explain.text: restore copies the last committed version of a file over your edits. revert adds a cancelling commit, so shared history is untouched. reset rewinds a branch, which is fine while the commits are yours alone.

screens.prose:
You staged two files, then decide plot.py should not be in this commit after all:

```sh
$ git add backtest.py plot.py
$ git restore --staged plot.py
```
screens.question: What happens to your edits in plot.py?

options.text: They stay in the file; it just leaves the staging area

options.why: That is plain `git restore plot.py`. With `--staged`, only the staging is undone.

options.text: They are committed on their own
options.why: restore never commits. It only changes what is staged or what is in a file.
restore acts only on the file you name.

hints.text: What does `--staged` restrict the command to?
This is the line the command changes.
`--staged` undoes the `git add` for that file and leaves its contents alone.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. `--staged` only touches the staging area.

explain.text: `git restore --staged plot.py` undoes the `git add` for that file. Your edits stay in the folder, so nothing is lost. Without `--staged`, restore would overwrite the edits.

screens.prose:
You have an hour of uncommitted edits in backtest.py. You also want to drop your last commit, c4, which only you have. You run:

```sh
$ git reset --hard HEAD~1
```

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

state.caption: Before the command, with uncommitted edits in the folder

screens.question: What happens to the hour of edits in backtest.py?

options.text: Gone for good: they were never committed, so Git has no copy
Safe: anything in Git can be undone
options.why: You trusted Git to keep everything. It can find lost commits, but these edits were never committed.

options.text: They move into the dropped commit, c4
options.why: A reset does not save anything. c4 holds only what it held before.

options.text: git refuses, because there are uncommitted changes
options.why: `--hard` does not ask. That is exactly why it is dangerous.

hints.text: Which work has Git ever saved: the commits, or the edits in your folder?
c4 is a commit, so Git keeps it somewhere. Your edits are not in any commit.
`--hard` rewrites the folder to match c3. Edits Git never saved are overwritten, with no way back.

feedback.correct: Committed work can be found again; uncommitted edits cannot.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether Git ever saved those edits.

byKey.undo: You trusted Git to keep everything. It can find lost commits, but these edits were never committed.

explain.text: `--hard` made the folder match c3 and overwrote your hour of edits. c4 can still be found with `git reflog`, because it was committed. Commit your work before any `--hard` reset.

canvas.caption: main moved to c3; the folder edits are gone

screens.prose:
The undo commands, from gentlest to roughest:

```sh
$ git restore --staged f   # unstage; edits kept
$ git revert HEAD          # cancel; safe if shared
$ git restore f            # edits overwritten
$ git reset --hard HEAD~1  # rewind; edits lost
```

Commits are hard to lose. Uncommitted edits are easy to lose.
screens.question: Which pair can destroy work that Git has no copy of?

options.why: revert only adds a commit. It never deletes anything.
`--staged` keeps your edits. Only plain restore overwrites them.

options.text: None: Git keeps a copy of everything
options.why: git keeps commits. Edits you never committed have no copy.

hints.text: Which commands rewrite the files in your folder?
Plain restore and `reset --hard` both overwrite the folder. Uncommitted edits there have no copy.

feedback.correct: Both overwrite uncommitted edits in your folder.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the commands that rewrite your folder.

explain.text: Plain `git restore` and `git reset --hard` overwrite files in the folder. Anything you had not committed is lost. Revert and `restore --staged` never touch your edits.

screens.prose: You meant to put a new volatility signal on its own branch, but committed it to main as c5. main must stay at c4, the version behind `results-2026-09.md`. Nobody else has c5 yet.

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

state.caption: c5 landed on main by accident

screens.question: Put the commands that fix this in order.

hints.text: Before main lets go of c5, what must point at it?
Right now only main reaches c5.
Label c5 with a new branch first. Then move main back one commit. Then switch to the new branch to carry on.

feedback.correct: Label c5, move main back, then switch to the new branch.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep c5 reachable before moving main.

byKey.reset: You moved main back before labelling c5. No branch would reach it, so your signal commit would be stranded.
byKey.switch: You switched to vol-signal before resetting, so the reset would move vol-signal back, not main.

explain.text: `git branch vol-signal` labels c5 and leaves HEAD on main. The reset then moves main back to c4, so it reproduces the results note again. Switching puts you on vol-signal, with the signal commit intact.

canvas.caption: main back on c4; the signal lives on vol-signal

ideas: `git restore` works on files you have not committed; `--staged` only unstages them.
`git revert` adds a commit that cancels another. Use it once anyone else has the commit.
`git reset --hard HEAD~1` moves the branch back one commit and overwrites the folder. Use it only on commits nobody else has.

formula.name: Undo a commit
formula.note: Uncommitted edits: `git restore`. Commit first: `--hard` destroys uncommitted edits for good.

summary.trap: git can find lost commits, but not edits you never committed. `reset --hard` and plain `restore` overwrite them with no way back.

quiz.question: Which commit is `HEAD~3`?

options.why: You took four steps. From c7: c6 is one, c5 two, c4 three.
That is HEAD~2. Take one more step.
The number counts steps back from HEAD, not commits from the start.

feedback.correct: Three parents back from c7 is c4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count arrows back from c7.

quiz.prose: A commit on main set transaction costs to zero by mistake. Two colleagues have already built branches on it.
quiz.question: Which command undoes it safely?

options.why: Their branches still contain the commit. Rewinding main makes the histories disagree, and the commit comes back when they merge.
restore discards uncommitted edits. The mistake is already committed.

options.text: Delete main and make it again
options.why: That loses every commit only main reaches, and still clashes with your colleagues' branches.

feedback.correct: revert adds a cancelling commit and rewrites nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Others have the commit already.

explain.text: Once others have a commit, only add to history. `git revert` makes a new commit that puts the costs back. Everyone's history still agrees.

quiz.prose: main has 4 commits. You run `git revert HEAD` to undo the last one.
quiz.question: How many commits does main contain afterwards?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does revert remove anything?

byKey.removed: You treated revert like reset. revert removes nothing; it adds one commit.
byKey.same: revert makes a new commit, so the count goes up by one.

explain.text: revert keeps all 4 commits and adds a fifth that cancels the last one. The files match commit 3. The history shows both the mistake and its undoing.

quiz.prose: You have been trying values in params.py all morning, none committed. None of them helped.
quiz.question: Which command puts params.py back to its last committed version?

options.why: That cancels the last commit, which was fine. Your trial edits are not in any commit.
That also drops your last commit, and overwrites every edited file, not just params.py.
`--staged` only unstages. Your edits would stay in the file.

feedback.correct: restore overwrites the file with its last committed version.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The edits are not committed, so work on the file.

explain.text: `git restore params.py` copies the committed version over your edits. Only that file changes. The morning's trial values are gone, which is what you wanted here.
